statement: Lecture 2 agenda: non-relational databases, then designing Slack's realtime (text) communication.
detail: 'Text' is written as an insertion under the agenda line.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Agenda : Non-relational databases / Designing : Slack's realtime communication / Text

statement: NoSQL means the data is structured non-relationally.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: NoSQL : Data is non-relational-ly structured

statement: In most cases NoSQL databases provide scalability and availability by compromising consistency.
detail: 'consistency' is highlighted on the board.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In most cases, NoSQL databases provide scalability and availability by compromising consistency.

statement: Most NoSQL databases are eventually consistent.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Most NoSQL DBs are eventually consistent

statement: NoSQL databases scaling does not mean SQL databases do not scale: anything that shards, scales.
detail: Boxed in pink with an arrow to 'anything that shards, scales'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: NoSQL DBs scale does not mean SQL does not -> anything that shards, scales

statement: Document databases are mostly JSON based.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Document DBs - Mostly JSON based

statement: Document databases support complex queries.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Supports complex queries

statement: Document databases allow partial updates to documents.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Partial updates to documents possible

statement: Document databases are the closest NoSQL type to a relational database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: closest to relational database

statement: Examples of document databases: MongoDB and ElasticSearch.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: MongoDB , ElasticSearch

statement: Key-value stores have a key-wise access pattern.
detail: Heading written 'Key Value stere' (= store).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Key Value stere - Key-wise access pattern

statement: Key-value stores are heavily partitioned.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Heavily partitioned

statement: Key-value stores do not support complex queries.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No complex queries supported

statement: Examples of key-value stores: Redis, DynamoDB, Aerospike.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis, DynamoDB, Aerospike

statement: Column-oriented databases are explained with a stock_ticks table with columns symbol, price, name, exchange, timestamp.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Table : stock_ticks  Symbol | price | name | exchange | timestamp

statement: A row-oriented database stores each row contiguously, while a column-oriented database stores each column's values together, so one row is spread across the column blocks.
detail: Diagram D-01: R1-R3 as long row blocks vs c1-c5 column blocks crossed by R1-R3 lines.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Row-oriented database / Column Oriented database

statement: Analytics example: a table with 100 columns and a query SELECT avg(price) WHERE ts = '...'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Say you have a table with 100 columns and you want to perform analytics SELECT avg(price) WHERE ts = '___';

statement: For that query only two columns matter (price and ts), but a row database goes row by row reading all columns and discarding 98 of them, which is inefficient.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But a row DB will go row by row reading all columns & discarding 98 of them [ inefficient ]

statement: Column-oriented databases read only the columns that are part of the query and do not even skim the others.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Column oriented databases will read columns that are part of the query and will not even skim others

statement: Hence column-oriented databases are used for massive analytics and data warehouses, e.g. Redshift.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Hence, column oriented DB are used in Massive analytics & data warehouses eg. RedShift

statement: Recommended reading: the foundational paper on column-oriented databases, 'C-Store: A Column Oriented DBMS'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Foundational paper on column oriented DB C-Store : A Column Oriented DBMS Do read this

statement: Graph databases store data in nodes and edges.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Graph Databases - stores data in nodes and edges

statement: Graph databases are great for modelling social behaviours and recommendations.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: great for modelling social behaviours, recommendations

statement: A solid use case for graph databases is fraud detection.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: solid use case: Fraud detection

statement: Examples of graph databases: Neo4j, Neptune, DGraph, TigerGraph.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: eg: Neo4j , Neptune , DGraph , TigerGraph

statement: Non-relational databases scale because there are no relations, data can be denormalized, and data is modelled to be sharded.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why non-relational DBs scale - There are no relations - Data can be denormalized - Data is modelled to be sharded

statement: The same can be achieved on SQL databases, so saying SQL does not scale is not entirely correct.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We can also achieve on SQL databases So, saying SQL does not scale is not entirely correct

statement: Use SQL when you need ACID, relations and constraints, and a fixed schema.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So, when to use SQL ? - ACID - Relations , Constraints - Fixed Schema

statement: Use NoSQL when there are no relations, data can be denormalized, and data can be sharded.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When to use NoSQL ? - No relations - Data can be denormalized - Data can be sharded

statement: Slack realtime communication requirements: multiple users and channels; users DM or message in a channel; real-time chat; historical messages can be scrolled through.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Requirements : Multiple users, Multiple channels - Users DM or message in channel - Real-time chat - Historical messages can be scrolled through

statement: Systems similar to Slack's realtime chat: multiplayer games, realtime chat, interactions, realtime polls, creator tools.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Similar Systems : Multiplayer games, realtime chat, interactions, realtime polls, creator tools, etc.

statement: Brainstormed entities: channels, messages, checkpoints, realtime communication, and membership.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Brainstorm : channels, messages, checkpoints, realtime communication (membership)

statement: Data model: users(id, name), channels(id, org, name, type), Membership(user_id, channel_id, checkpoint), Messages(from, channel_id, created_at, msg).
detail: Built live 01:04-01:17 (D-02); created_at is scrawled on the board.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: users id name / channels id org name / Membership user_id channel_id / Messages from channel_id msg

statement: First messages schema: sender_id, channel_id, receiver_id and msg, where a message goes either to a DM or a channel.
detail: Erased and replaced step by step: from + to (ch/usr), then from/to/type, then from + channel_id (01:08-01:11).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: sender_id channel_id receiver_id msg -> DM / ch

statement: The join table is named 'Membership' rather than 'user.channel'.
detail: 'user.channel' written first at ~01:05 and replaced by 'Membership' by 01:06.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: user.channel -> Membership

statement: A DM is modelled as a channel with 2 people.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: DM = channel with 2 people

statement: Channels get a type field: group, user (DM) or regular channel.
detail: Written 'type : grp/user/ch', later 'reg' over 'ch'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: type : grp/user/reg

statement: The membership table stores a checkpoint (how far the user has read in the channel).
detail: Board shows only '[ checkpoint ]'; the meaning is from the audio.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: [ checkpoint ]

statement: Message store options listed for the high-level design: MySQL, Cassandra, Mongo.
detail: Label reads 'MySQL / Cassanda / Mongo' (Mongo cut at the edge in early frames).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: MySQL / Cassanda / Mongo

statement: Clients send messages to API servers and keep a separate WebSocket connection to WebSocket servers.
detail: D-03: A,B -> API stack; yellow arcs from A to the WS stack.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: API / WS

statement: Frequent communication means a socket is definitely needed.
detail: Board: 'Socket ??' then 'Defintly' and 'Freq Commⁿ' (abbreviations).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Socket ?? Defintly Freq Commⁿ

statement: There are three ways to persist a message on the same architecture: (1) persist synchronously through the API servers, then deliver; (2) send over WebSocket to the edge server and persist asynchronously through Kafka and workers; (3) deliver over WebSocket with no persistence.
detail: D-04, markers 1-3; colours white/green/blue.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 3 ways to persist the message

statement: Depending on how critical persistence is, pick one of the three approaches over the others.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Depending on criticality of "persistence" we pick one over other

statement: Each WebSocket server has a connection limit; the example assumes 4, so the 5th member of Channel 1 (E) connects to a second server WS2.
detail: WS1 drawn with four yellow dots (connections).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Channel 1 - A - B - C - D - E  WS1  WS2

statement: Each WebSocket server keeps the membership of its connected users: WS1 knows A, B, C, D are in C1; WS2 knows E is in C1.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: WS1 -> A->C1 B->C1 C->C1 D->C1  WS2 E->C1

statement: To reach a member on another WebSocket server, connect the two servers with a plain TCP connection and forward the message.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: TCP

statement: Adding more WebSocket servers with TCP links between every pair turns into a full mesh of connections.
detail: D-05 final mesh; audio discusses the overhead.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: TCP

statement: Replace the mesh with a realtime Pub/Sub (Redis): every WebSocket server keeps one connection to it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis Realtime PubSub

statement: A WebSocket server subscribes to the Pub/Sub channel of each Slack channel its users belong to (WS1 -> SUB(C1), WS2 -> SUB(C1)); a server whose users are only in C2 does not get C1 messages.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: WS1 -> SUB(C1)  WS2 -> SUB(C1)  G -> C2  H -> C2

statement: A separate balancer service tells a client which WebSocket server to connect to (it balances the connections).
detail: Purple box and arrows next to A; label 'Balance Connectn'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Balance Connectn

statement: Insight 1: DMs are channels with 2 people, so only channels need to be modelled very well.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Insight 1 : DMs are channel with 2 people  Thus we only need to model channels very well

statement: A Slack workspace has multiple channels, each with multiple messages.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: workspace -> multiple channels -> multiple messages

statement: Recap schema: workspace(id, name); channels(id, workspace_id, name, type); messages(id, channel_id, message, user_id, ts); membership(channel_id, user_id, checkpoint).
detail: ', type' added live at 02:19:45.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: workspace id, name / channels id, workspace_id, name , type / messages id, channel_id, message, user_id, ts

statement: Because there will be a large number of messages, store them in a sharded database; pick any database you can shard, even SQL works.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we store it in a sharded DB pick any DB that you can shard .... even SQL works !

statement: Shard messages by channel_id into mutually exclusive shards, so all messages of a channel are in one database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: mutually exclusive - sharded by channel_id All messages of a channel in one DB

statement: With all of a channel's messages in one shard, scrolling is simple and needs no cross-shard query.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: scrolling is simple, no cross shard query

statement: Basic flow: send_message(from_user, to_channel, text) is a REST call to the messaging service; the API server finds the relevant shard using channel_id and stores the message there.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: send_message ( from_user, to_channel, text ) : REST CALL API server find relevant shard using channel_id and store message there

statement: This basic flow solves sending messages for both DMs and channels.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we solve sending messages for both DM & channel

statement: REST-based short polling is a very poor UX for something as realtime as messaging, so a better solution is needed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: REST based short polling is a very poor UX for something as realtime as messaging .... so, we need a better solution

statement: Every user has one WebSocket connection open with the backend, used for anything and everything realtime; it is a persistent TCP connection.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every user will have 1 websocket connection open with our backend infrastructure and that will be used for anything and everything realtime

statement: WebSockets are expensive and browsers have a 6 concurrent TCP connection limit, so all realtime communication must be multiplexed on ONE WebSocket connection.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because WebSockets are expensive and browsers have a 6 concurrent TCP connection limit We have to multiplex all realtime communication on ONE WEBSOCKET connection

statement: Hence a fleet of edge servers is needed, to which end users connect over WebSocket.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Hence, we need a fleet of servers ( Edge Servers ) to whom our end users connect over WS

statement: Any service (chat, notifications, etc.) that wants to talk to users in realtime sends the information through the edge servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Any service chat, notification, etc wants to talk to users in realtime the info will go through these edge servers

statement: In the Kafka path, messages go from the edge server into Kafka and messaging-service workers persist them to the partitioned messages DB; a separate messaging service serves reads.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Edge Server Kafka Messaging Service workers Messages DB (partitioned) Messaging Svc

statement: Insight: messages once sent will always be persisted; there will be no DB-level runtime exception such as a unique-key failure.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Insight : Messages once sent will always be persisted, there will not be any DB level runtime exception like Unique Key failed, etc

statement: Non-realtime use cases (channel scroll, DM scroll, unimportant messages loaded when a channel is clicked, e.g. muted channels) go through the REST messaging service: anything that is not pushed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Non-realtime usecases - channel scroll - DM scroll - unimportant messages ... eg: Muted channels

statement: Idea: every Slack channel has one Pub/Sub channel, and each edge server subscribes to the Pub/Sub channels of the Slack channels its connected users are part of.
detail: Noted on the board: '* can be optimized'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every Slach channel has one PubSub channel Each edge server subscribes to the PubSub channel corresponding to the slack channels ...

statement: Example: A in c1,c2,c3; B in c2,c4,c5; C in c1,c3; D in c4, all on one edge server, which subscribes to c1..c5 on the realtime Pub/Sub (Redis).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: SUB(c1,c2,c3,c4,c5) Realtime PubSub [Redis]

statement: A message that is not delivered in realtime must not be dropped: the client loads messages through the channel-scroll REST API when the channel is clicked, as a correction.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We cannot drop the message, hence we can use the channel scroll API ( REST ) to load the messages when channel is clicked

statement: For missed realtime messages (a transient issue): (1) a correction job ensures messages are shown; (2) buffer messages in another Kafka and replay them when sockets are back up.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 1. Remember we have correction job ! ... 2. Buffer the messages in another kafka and when sockets are back up, we replay them

statement: Overall architecture: users on WebSocket to edge servers (holding membership), edge servers linked by a clustered Redis Pub/Sub, edge servers writing to Kafka, workers persisting to a partitioned messages DB, a load-balanced API server fleet for non-realtime APIs, and a balancer telling users which edge server to use.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Overall architecture Edge Servers Redis PubSub [clustered] Kafka Messaging Service workers Messages DB (partitioned) API Servers Balancer

statement: API servers handle non-realtime APIs, channel scroll and muted channels.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: API Servers - non-realtime API - channel scroll - mutd channels

statement: If each server handles 4 users, the 5th user forms a WebSocket with another server; a message from A to B goes through the local connection pool, but A to E is possible only when the message reaches Edge Server 2.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The 5th user forms a websocket with another server ... Possible only when message reaches Edge Server 2

statement: Connecting every one of 100 edge servers to every other is not a great idea; a realtime Pub/Sub does better.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But if we have 100 Edge Server will every server to every another server ? Not a great Idea ! Can we do better ?

statement: Every edge server knows which users are connected to it and how to communicate with them (a local connection pool managed by the Socket.IO library).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every edge server knows which user is connected to it and how to communicate with it [ Socket IO library manages this ]

statement: When a message is sent from A to B, the edge server persists it in Kafka, finds B in the local pool, and sends the message to B.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 1. Persist message In Kafka 2. Find B in the local pool 3. Send message to B
